title: Plan B

jokes.text: I know. I broke it. I needed to speak with you, and I knew that was the fastest way to get you up here.
jokes.setup: Liz storms in angry about the vending machine being broken
jokes.punchline: Jack casually admits he broke it on purpose to summon Liz, knowing food is her greatest motivator
jokes.explanation: An excellent cold-open joke that does heavy character work in two lines. Jack's Machiavellian willingness to break a vending machine to manipulate Liz, and Liz's utter predictability around food, are both perfectly distilled. The 'You bastard! I trusted you!' reaction is the implicit third beat — Liz's outrage is at the betrayal, not the machine, which tells us everything about her relationship to food and to Jack.

jokes.text: You bastard! I trusted you!
jokes.setup: Jack reveals he broke the vending machine on purpose
jokes.punchline: Liz's response frames the broken vending machine as a profound personal betrayal, not a trivial inconvenience
jokes.explanation: Four words that contain an entire character portrait. The word 'trusted' does the work — it implies a solemn, deeply held faith in the vending machine's availability. The comic logic is that Liz's relationship with food is as emotionally weighted as any human bond.

jokes.text: I'm doing God's work here in Africa. Why, just yesterday, I kicked two naked people out of a garden!
jokes.setup: Tracy claims he is doing God's work in Africa
jokes.punchline: His example of 'God's work' is literally re-enacting the expulsion from the Garden of Eden, which he presents as an unambiguously good deed
jokes.explanation: A gem. The setup 'God's work' is broadly noble-sounding, but the punchline reframes it as recreating a Biblical expulsion — which Tracy presents with complete sincerity. The joke works on two levels: Tracy's obliviousness and the absurdist image of him wandering Africa kicking naked people out of gardens. The Biblical allusion is just specific enough to reward attentive viewers without being smug. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Simba, Rafiki! Click, click, click! Yeah, that's right, I just put you in your place in African.
jokes.setup: Tracy is being urged to return to TGS but ignores the plea
jokes.punchline: He shouts Lion King character names and clicking sounds as if speaking an African language, then congratulates himself on linguistic dominance
jokes.explanation: Pure Tracy. The joke layers multiple absurdities: using Lion King character names as language, treating Xhosa-style clicks as vocabulary, and the supreme confidence with which he declares victory. 'I just put you in your place in African' is the perfect button — he has no idea 'African' is not a language, and his pride is total. Only Tracy Jordan could deliver this.

jokes.text: 'TGS with Tracy Jordan' without Tracy Jordan is an oxymoron, like 'liberal government' or 'female scientist.'
jokes.setup: Jack explains the semantic problem of running TGS without Tracy
jokes.punchline: His examples of 'oxymorons' are 'liberal government' and 'female scientist' — things that are only oxymorons to a man of Jack's particular worldview
jokes.explanation: A classic Jack Donaghy joke structure: making a reasonable rhetorical point and then revealing his retrograde worldview through the examples he chooses. The joke isn't that he's wrong about TGS — he's not — but that his parallel examples expose his politics and attitudes toward women so naturally. The escalation from 'liberal government' (political) to 'female scientist' (personal bias) lands perfectly.

jokes.text: Or 'Princeton football.' We were four and three in Ivy League play last year! Our quarterback, Henry Chang...
jokes.setup: Jack's list of oxymorons invites a third example
jokes.punchline: Someone defensively adds 'Princeton football' as an oxymoron, then immediately undermines themselves by citing their actual record with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: A neat surprise — someone in the room adds 'Princeton football' to the oxymoron list, presumably as self-deprecating Ivy League humor, but then pivots immediately to defending Princeton football's record with complete sincerity. The pivot is the joke. 'It doesn't matter' from Jack cutting him off is a good button.

jokes.text: Power wagging, and I'm doing what I can, but I spent a lot of political capital buying a new network for KableTown.
jokes.setup: Liz asks if Jack is 'power wagging' (gesturing at desks) and whether he's fighting for the show
jokes.punchline: Jack names the gesture 'power wagging' without irony and pivots to explain his political constraints
jokes.explanation: The visual gag of Liz's 'what is this called?' pantomime plus Jack immediately having a name for it ('power wagging') is a small but efficient moment of character comedy. Jack's world has terminology for everything.

jokes.text: Is it TNT? Are Rizzoli and Isles friends in real life?
jokes.setup: Jack mentions buying a new network
jokes.punchline: Liz's first instinct is to ask about a procedural drama's cast's off-screen friendship — a completely irrelevant non-sequitur that reveals her pop-culture-obsessed mind
jokes.explanation: Liz cuts through a corporate moment with a completely sincere celebrity-friendship question. It's a good Liz-character joke — she's always more interested in pop-culture minutiae than professional concerns. The specificity of 'Rizzoli and Isles' elevates it above a generic celebrity-gossip gag.

jokes.text: TWINKS is an acronym designed to project a positive gay image. 'TWINKS... Television With Individuals... Naive, Kinky, Shaved.'
jokes.setup: Liz points out that 'twink' is a term for a young, hairless gay man; Jack insists it's an acronym
jokes.punchline: The acronym Jack reveals is, if anything, worse than the slang term — 'Naive, Kinky, Shaved' is both offensive and absurd as a 'positive image'
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's strongest jokes. The structure is a classic misdirection: Jack defends 'TWINKS' as a wholesome acronym, which raises expectations of a PR-safe solution, and then the actual expansion — 'Naive, Kinky, Shaved' — is exactly as bad as what it was supposedly replacing, and arguably worse. The word 'Naive' sitting between 'Kinky' and 'Shaved' is the comedic peak. Jack delivers it with total earnestness, which makes it land harder. High quotability, strong rewatch value.

jokes.text: Ugh, no. Next. [Reacting to bad TWINKS programming on screen]
jokes.setup: Jack describes TWINKS struggling to find its footing
jokes.punchline: A visual cut to whatever awful programming Jack is watching, punctuated by his disgusted 'Ugh, no. Next' — the reaction sells the gag
jokes.explanation: A reaction beat that works primarily as a visual gag — we infer Jack is flipping through terrible programming. The humor is in the casualness of 'Next' as a full rejection. Functional but not a standout.

jokes.text: When I was with D'Fwan on 'Queen of Jordan,' he spent $4,000 on chihuahua outfits for himself.
jokes.setup: Liz argues that gay male viewers are coveted by advertisers
jokes.punchline: Her example of disposable gay income is D'Fwan buying $4,000 worth of chihuahua outfits — for himself, not a chihuahua
jokes.explanation: The beat where 'for himself' is delivered as a separate sentence fragment is the entire joke — the listener assumes chihuahua outfits means dressing a chihuahua, and the correction is both funnier and stranger. The D'Fwan character adds specificity; this isn't just a generic gay joke but a reference to an established character's established absurdity. The chihuahua detail will also callback later, earning rewatch bonus.

jokes.text: 'I'm Afraid My Hands Are Tied'... is the only show anyone's watching on TWINKS.
jokes.setup: Jack says 'I'm afraid my hands are tied' as an expression of helplessness about TGS
jokes.punchline: He reveals mid-phrase that it's also the title of the only successful show on TWINKS — a bondage double entendre delivered straight
jokes.explanation: One of the best-constructed jokes in the episode. It's a pure misdirection: the phrase starts as a standard idiom, and the pivot to it being a show title happens mid-sentence in a way the audience doesn't see coming. The implication that TWINKS's only hit is a bondage-themed show adds a second layer. Economy is exceptional — maximum information in minimum words. The structure earns a 9 because the delivery timing is built into the writing itself.

jokes.text: Sidney, it's Frank. 'TGS' is dead. Start booking me stand-up gigs. How many black women's colleges are there in the country?
jokes.setup: Liz announces to the writers that the hiatus is temporary; Frank immediately gets on the phone
jokes.punchline: Frank has already concluded TGS is dead, is pivoting to stand-up at black women's colleges — a self-aware joke about his extreme inappropriateness as a comedian for that demographic
jokes.explanation: Frank's immediate defection and his specific, wildly inappropriate career target is good character comedy. The question 'How many black women's colleges are there?' implies he's doing market sizing for a demographic utterly misaligned with him, which is funny in its obliviousness. 'Harriet Tubman School of Nursing? Yes and yes!' landing as the button seals it.

jokes.text: Last time I taught, I was like Robin Williams in 'Dead Poets Society,' by which I mean I got fired.
jokes.setup: Pete says he can go back to substitute teaching since he kept his certificate
jokes.punchline: Comparing himself to Robin Williams in Dead Poets Society sounds inspirational, but the clarification reveals the comparison is only about getting fired
jokes.explanation: A well-structured two-beat joke. The 'by which I mean' construction is a reliable 30 Rock device, but it's earned here because the clarification genuinely subverts the flattering comparison. Pete's self-awareness about the actual outcome (firing) vs. the implied outcome (inspirational teaching) is funny and characterful.

jokes.text: No, I meant my JennaBabies and I will get through this. I've been selling these on QVC for years. It's my Plan B.
jokes.setup: Liz thanks someone for having faith; the person responds warmly — but it's Jenna
jokes.punchline: Jenna clarifies she meant herself and her JennaBabies dolls, which she's been selling on QVC — she has a thriving mercenary backup plan and cares nothing about TGS
jokes.explanation: Good Jenna character comedy — her warmth is entirely self-directed, and her Plan B being a doll line she's already been running for years is perfectly mercenary. The misdirect of 'we'll get through this' being about her QVC business rather than TGS is well-set-up.

jokes.text: This is Asian JennaBaby. Excuse me, G.I., do you miss your girlfriend? I'm good at math. So it's not offensive.
jokes.setup: Jenna shows off her Asian JennaBaby doll
jokes.punchline: The doll's demonstration consists of three consecutive Asian stereotypes delivered in sequence, followed by Jenna's sincere belief that math proficiency cancels out the offense
jokes.explanation: The escalating stereotype structure — G.I. girlfriend trope, math achievement — works because Jenna presents it as a rebuttal to the obvious criticism, not the criticism itself. 'So it's not offensive' is the perfect button: she has performed the offense and then declared it cancelled. Only Jenna would create this product and sell it on QVC. Strong character integration and dark enough to generate nervous laughter.

jokes.text: I'm going back to the job I had in Holland... police psychic. A Dutch TV show is based on me.
jokes.setup: Writers are announcing their Plan Bs
jokes.punchline: One writer's backup career is Dutch police psychic, which is specific, dignified, and completely insane
jokes.explanation: The specificity of Holland, police psychic, and a Dutch TV show based on this person is the joke's entire engine. It's not explained or dwelt on, which is the right call — the absurdity is presented as mundane biographical fact. Good economy.

jokes.text: With my degree, I can always go into architecture or medical nanotechnology... I'm sorry, I don't understand. Oh. I see. At Harvard, we call them 'concentrations'...
jokes.setup: Liz asks Toofer what he majored in; he lists impressive career options
jokes.punchline: When asked what he majored in, he doesn't understand the word 'major' because at Harvard they're called 'concentrations' — a pompous distinction that lands as pure snobbery
jokes.explanation: Classic Toofer — his Harvard credentials come with insufferable terminological precision. The pause where he genuinely doesn't understand the word 'major' is a perfect character beat. It's a well-worn joke type (Ivy League elitism) but the specific execution with 'concentrations' is sharp.

jokes.text: Let me just take out my idea journal. Hmm. This just says 'Bird Internet.'
jokes.setup: Liz promises she can save the show and reaches for her idea journal
jokes.punchline: The journal contains only the words 'Bird Internet' — a conceptually meaningless phrase that she wrote down at some point as if it were a serious idea
jokes.explanation: 'Bird Internet' is one of the episode's standout absurdist moments. It's a non-idea presented as the sole contents of a dedicated idea journal, which says everything about Liz's creative limitations and her self-delusion about them. The phrase 'Bird Internet' is funny because it sounds like it could mean something but doesn't. It also sets up a running callback that pays off beautifully at the episode's end. Economy score is nearly perfect — two words do enormous work.

jokes.text: Simon, you're my agent. You're not supposed to panic. You're supposed to help me. Like how Fredward helps iCarly.
jokes.setup: Liz's agent panics about the hiatus
jokes.punchline: Liz's reference point for agent-client loyalty is Fredward from iCarly — a children's show character — revealing her media diet
jokes.explanation: The iCarly reference is good character work for Liz — it reveals she watches and takes emotional notes from children's programming. The 'No!' button from Simon adds to it. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Liz's agent Simon panics immediately when he hears 'forced hiatus.'
jokes.setup: Liz asks her agent Simon not to panic and to help her find her Plan B.
jokes.punchline: Simon panics immediately despite being told not to, suggesting the hiatus is as bad as everyone fears.
jokes.explanation: Functional joke — the agent panicking confirms the stakes while being mildly amusing. Not particularly original but serves the scene. Competent setup for Simon's later behavior.

jokes.text: Would you be willing to come in for an Alpo commercial? If you can get through the audition without pooping, it's yours.
jokes.setup: Liz asks her agent to find her a writing job
jokes.punchline: He offers her a dog food commercial audition with the qualification that she must not poop during it
jokes.explanation: The bar Simon sets — not pooping — is the joke. It implies previous auditioners have failed this minimum standard. The agent offering a dog food commercial as the best option for Liz is also a solid beat. 'I'm a human writer, Simon' as her response is a good capper.

jokes.text: Baby? Ah, yes, BAB Y... Black-Asian Bisexual Youths. Those are viewers we want, and TWINKS is gonna bring them in.
jokes.setup: Jack's colleague asks about 'the baby' as a personal question
jokes.punchline: Jack immediately reframes 'baby' as a demographic acronym, pivoting away from the personal and into the professional — his daughter reduced to a business category
jokes.explanation: The joke works on a character level: Jack's instinct is to convert every word into business language, including the word 'baby.' The acronym itself ('Black-Asian Bisexual Youths') is constructed well — it sounds like a real ad-industry demographic segment. Good character integration.

jokes.text: My night nurse swears she calls me 'koskel,' which, in Trinidadian Creole, means 'stranger.'
jokes.setup: Jack's colleague asks about his baby daughter Liddy
jokes.punchline: The only thing Liddy apparently says to Jack is a word for 'stranger' — his own infant daughter doesn't recognize him as her father
jokes.explanation: A quietly devastating joke about Jack's emotional unavailability and absenteeism as a father. The specificity of 'Trinidadian Creole' and 'koskel' makes it feel researched and particular rather than generic. Jack delivers it without self-pity or awareness of how damning it is, which is the most Jack thing possible. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Jack, there's lots of things I like... fishing, marches by John Philip Sousa, telephones that look like footballs. But there's one thing I don't like... losing money!
jokes.setup: Hank is dressing down Jack about TWINKS losing money
jokes.punchline: His list of likes — fishing, Sousa marches, football-shaped phones — paints him as an endearingly specific old-school American, making the pivot to fury about money funnier
jokes.explanation: Hank Hooper's character is entirely built through specificity. The list of likes is curated perfectly — each item is more specific than the last, culminating in 'telephones that look like footballs,' which is both a real product and an incredibly precise characterization. The contrast with his business fury makes the list land harder.

jokes.text: I don't know if my tone is conveying the fury I feel about this, but I am, pardon my French... bonjour.
jokes.setup: Hank says he's very angry and about to say something rude — 'pardon my French'
jokes.punchline: His 'French' is just 'bonjour' — the most benign French word possible, which undercuts the threat entirely
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the episode and arguably a contender for an 8+ comparison to the anchors. The structure is near-perfect: 'pardon my French' is a well-worn idiom that primes the audience to expect profanity. The subversion — 'bonjour' — is maximally surprising while being maximally simple. The joke also characterizes Hank beautifully: he's too decent to actually swear, so his 'fury' manifests as a greeting. The subsequent acknowledgment ('Now, that's a joke, but I am really, really mad!') is a self-aware button that works in its own right. Exceptional economy — one word does all the work. Near-top quotability.

jokes.text: Now, that's a joke, but I am really, really mad!
jokes.setup: Hank delivers the 'bonjour' joke
jokes.punchline: He immediately breaks frame to clarify it was a joke while insisting his anger is real — the meta-acknowledgment is itself funny because it ruins and re-sells the joke simultaneously
jokes.explanation: The meta-commentary on his own joke is a nice secondary beat. Hank explaining that he was joking but is genuinely furious works because it's so earnest — he wants credit for the wit and also wants the anger registered. Good Hank characterization.

jokes.text: I'm remaking 'Knight Rider' with the Oscar Mayer Wienermobile.
jokes.setup: Jack claims he's already working on fixing TWINKS
jokes.punchline: His programming solution is a Knight Rider remake where the car is replaced by the Wienermobile
jokes.explanation: Absurdist television pitch comedy. The Wienermobile as K.I.T.T. is a specific, visual, immediately funny image. Jack pitching it with the same gravity he'd use for a genuine programming decision is the character integration. Short, punchy, memorable.

jokes.text: You made a bad decision and bought something you didn't understand, like when I bought tickets for 'Black Swan.' Remember when a movie was just a fella with a hat running away from a fella with no hair?
jokes.setup: Hank chastises Jack for buying TWINKS
jokes.punchline: He compares it to his own bad decision — buying Black Swan tickets — and his description of classic cinema ('a fella with a hat running away from a fella with no hair') is a perfectly innocent reductive summary
jokes.explanation: Hank's film criticism is characterful and specific — Black Swan as his most confusing cultural experience. His nostalgic description of old Hollywood is both reductive and specific enough to be funny. 'A fella with a hat' could be Cary Grant, Humphrey Bogart, or Indiana Jones, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: ...unless there's a gay Jack Donaghy locked up somewhere who understands all this stuff, let's just chalk this one up to never again.
jokes.setup: Hank is suggesting they abandon TWINKS entirely
jokes.punchline: He inadvertently describes exactly what Jack is about to propose (Devon Banks), framing it as a joke about an impossible hypothetical
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed dramatic irony joke — Hank's hypothetical perfectly describes Devon Banks, and Jack's immediate 'Hank... there IS a gay Jack Donaghy' is a great button. The audience knows the answer before Jack says it, which creates a satisfying anticipation beat.

jokes.text: His name is Devon Banks. [Beat] I sense something, a presence I've not felt since...
jokes.setup: Jack reveals Devon Banks exists and is the solution
jokes.punchline: The cut to a dramatic Star Wars-style reaction beat — a 'presence' being felt — played completely straight for the reveal of a TV nemesis
jokes.explanation: The Star Wars 'I sense a presence' parody applied to a corporate TV nemesis is a fun genre mash. The ellipsis (the unfinished 'since...') mimics Obi-Wan's famous line from A New Hope. It's a quick, self-aware gag that escalates the stakes of Banks's arrival comically.

jokes.text: Banks? But he's your nemesis. That would be like me hiring that mouse that keeps pooping in my slippers!
jokes.setup: Jack announces he'll hire Devon Banks
jokes.punchline: Liz's analogy for a nemesis is a mouse that poops in her slippers — a domestic, unglamorous image compared to the corporate espionage context
jokes.explanation: Liz's analogy is perfectly scaled to her life — while Jack operates in the world of corporate sharks, her nemesis is literal vermin in her apartment. The specificity of 'pooping in my slippers' is good Liz-character detail. The bathos of the comparison is the joke.

jokes.text: He's a gay shark, like the actor who played Jaws.
jokes.setup: Jack describes Devon Banks as dangerous
jokes.punchline: The metaphor 'gay shark' is followed by a bizarre clarification — 'like the actor who played Jaws' — implying the mechanical shark from the movie was gay, or that there was a gay actor in a shark suit
jokes.explanation: The joke hinges on the absurdity of 'the actor who played Jaws' — the shark in Jaws was a mechanical prop, not an actor. Jack's complete sincerity in offering this as a meaningful clarification is the character comedy. It's a quick, sharp absurdist beat.

jokes.text: Banks put all of his eggs in the Obama basket. When the administration started to falter because of our conspiracy... I mean, Obama's ineptitude...
jokes.setup: Jack explains Devon's political fall from grace
jokes.punchline: Jack accidentally says 'our conspiracy' and immediately self-corrects to 'Obama's ineptitude' — a Freudian slip confirming what was previously only implied
jokes.explanation: An excellent political joke delivered through character. The slip-and-correction structure is a classic device, but the content — Jack casually admitting to a conspiracy to sabotage a president before catching himself — is peak 30 Rock in its dark satire. The correction to 'Obama's ineptitude' is itself a political joke. Great character integration; this is completely Jack.

jokes.text: Then he tried to rejoin us capitalists. Showed up at John Paulson's Sweet Sixteen Billion party. Nobody would talk to him, not even Ira. And he was all, 'Oh, I'll just look at these books,' then pretended to get a text and left. And we were all like, 'Whatever. We'll go to IHOP and not tell him!'
jokes.setup: Jack narrates Devon's social fall from grace among the ultra-wealthy
jokes.punchline: The social dynamics of billionaires play out exactly like middle school drama — fake texting to escape an awkward party, going to IHOP without inviting someone
jokes.explanation: The joke works through comedic register juxtaposition: the ultra-wealthy world of hedge funds and 'Sweet Sixteen Billion' parties is described with the petty social mechanics of a high school cafeteria. 'Not even Ira' adds a humanizing detail to the billionaire clique. 'We'll go to IHOP and not tell him' is the perfect button — the world's richest people snubbing someone at IHOP is both absurdist and somehow exactly believable.

jokes.text: He's on LinkedIn, Lemon. He might as well be dead!
jokes.setup: Jack tracks Devon Banks down to Brooklyn
jokes.punchline: Devon's presence on LinkedIn — a professional networking site — is treated as a sign of complete social and professional death
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect economy. LinkedIn is the butt of the joke because it's the site people join when they're desperate for work — and in the world of the ultra-powerful, even that mild professional humiliation is equivalent to death. The delivery ('He might as well be dead!') escalates it from a mild observation to a declaration of ruin. High quotability; this line works out of context.

jokes.text: ...crab, I guess. What else crawls, Lemon? Babies, Jack. You have one.
jokes.setup: Jack searches for the right animal metaphor for Devon 'crawling' back
jokes.punchline: When Liz answers his rhetorical question ('Babies, Jack'), the answer doubles as a reminder of his parental neglect
jokes.explanation: A compact two-line exchange that does double duty: it's a funny non-sequitur ('what else crawls?') with an unexpected answer, and the answer is simultaneously a punchline and a character revelation about Jack's distance from his infant daughter. 'Babies, Jack. You have one.' is a genuinely sharp line.

jokes.text: Speaking of TV ideas, would you buy a show about a girl television writer trying to have it all in the city and also she's a vampire, I guess?
jokes.setup: Liz pivots mid-conversation to pitch Jack a show
jokes.punchline: The show is obviously Liz's own life with 'vampire' tacked on as a half-hearted trend hook — the 'I guess' reveals her complete lack of commitment to her own pitch
jokes.explanation: Meta-referential in that the show Liz is pitching is clearly 30 Rock with a vampire element. The 'I guess' is the key word — she's pitching a vampire show without any conviction about the vampire part, because it's clearly just an industry trend she's bolting on. Jack's response ('I like the end part') is a perfect button. The joke also serves as commentary on the vampire TV oversaturation of the era.

jokes.text: I like the end part.
jokes.setup: Liz pitches 'a girl television writer trying to have it all... also she's a vampire, I guess'
jokes.punchline: Jack ignores the show concept entirely and endorses only the vampire element — dismissing everything Liz represents as a premise
jokes.explanation: Four words, perfect economy. Jack's preference for the vampire twist over Liz's actual (autobiographical) premise is a quietly devastating critique of network television and of Liz's lack of commercial appeal as a protagonist. Works as a standalone deadpan line and as a callback button.

jokes.text: I thought we understood each other! I thought we understood that you are never to think that I understand anything!
jokes.setup: Liz says she thought they had an understanding about the meaning of 'forced hiatus'
jokes.punchline: Jack's correction of the misunderstanding is itself a paradox — 'we understood that you are never to think I understand anything' — his rule is that Liz should assume his total inscrutability
jokes.explanation: A satisfying logical paradox delivered at speed. Jack's correction is self-defeating — he's articulating the rule clearly, which undermines the rule. The escalating frustration of both characters makes this land. Good character work for Jack's expectation of Liz's deference.

jokes.text: Well, there have been a lot of 'Amazing Races' on since then, and I had to watch them and go online and comment on them!
jokes.setup: Jack points out he's been warning Liz to prepare a Plan B for two years
jokes.punchline: Liz's excuse for not preparing is that she was busy watching and online-commenting on The Amazing Race — a reality show about other people's preparation and action
jokes.explanation: Liz's procrastination excuse — watching a show about people taking action rather than taking action herself — has a nice ironic layer. The specificity of going online to comment adds to her portrait of someone who engages with life through media rather than directly.

jokes.text: Olive just turns into Barham? Justice for Rodney King! How do I get to 10? It's the 10! Rodney King!
jokes.setup: Jack suggests Liz go to L.A.; Liz has clearly been to L.A. once and retained only confused road memories and a Rodney King non-sequitur
jokes.punchline: Her entire experience of L.A. is getting lost on the freeway and shouting 'Rodney King!' as a driving exclamation
jokes.explanation: The joke is structured as a rapid-fire recreation of Liz's internal L.A. monologue — she conflates freeway confusion with social justice, and shouts 'Rodney King' as if it's a driving incantation rather than a meaningful political statement. The repetition builds nicely. It's a fast, committed absurdist beat.

jokes.text: What about opportunities for storytellers? Beginning with the cave paintings of Lascaux, mankind...
jokes.setup: Jack says opportunities for writers are fewer and farther between
jokes.punchline: Liz's reframe of 'writer' as 'storyteller' and her immediate invocation of prehistoric cave paintings to defend her irrelevance is both pompous and self-defeating
jokes.explanation: Liz's pivot from 'writer' to 'storyteller' and her invocation of Lascaux is a good portrait of a mediocre person inflating their self-concept with grand historical precedent. The joke is cut off before she can finish the speech, which is the right call — we don't need it.

jokes.text: I'm Aaron Sorkin. 'The West Wing,' 'A Few Good Men,' 'The Social Network.' — 'Studio 60.' — Shut up.
jokes.setup: Liz meets a fellow writer waiting for the Nick Lachey meeting
jokes.punchline: The man introduces himself as Aaron Sorkin and lists his credits; Liz (or someone) interjects 'Studio 60' — his notable flop — and Sorkin immediately shuts it down
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best gags. Aaron Sorkin playing himself and listing his prestige credits — West Wing, Few Good Men, Social Network — builds an impressive CV, and then the interruption with 'Studio 60' (his universally acknowledged failure at the time) is the perfect deflation. 'Shut up' is the ideal response: defensive, abrupt, self-aware. The joke works on industry-insider and general audience levels. Sorkin's willingness to make himself the butt of the joke adds to its impact. High quotability and rewatch value.

jokes.text: Our craft is dying while people are playing Angry Birds and poking each other on Facebook! What is poking anyway? Why won't anybody do it to me? I'm cool!
jokes.setup: Sorkin delivers an impassioned speech about the death of the writing craft
jokes.punchline: His noble lament about digital distraction collapses into a personal grievance about not being poked on Facebook — revealing his own desperate need for social validation
jokes.explanation: The shift from 'our craft is dying' grandeur to 'why won't anybody poke me' petulance is a perfect comic deflation. It humanizes Sorkin hilariously — his concern about digital culture isn't philosophical, it's personal rejection. 'I'm cool!' as a defense is the most uncool possible thing to say. Works especially well as a Sorkin character joke given his reputation for grandiosity.

jokes.text: Speaking of Angry Birds, do you know how to beat 11-4? It's just a red guy and a green guy. The key is do not use the green guy as a boomerang.
jokes.setup: Sorkin has just given an impassioned speech about people wasting time on Angry Birds
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately pivots to asking for Angry Birds tips, proving his entire point — and she has specific level knowledge
jokes.explanation: Excellent comedic structure: Sorkin's speech sets up the ironic fall by naming Angry Birds as the enemy of craft, and Liz immediately proves his point by being more interested in the game than the conversation. The level-specific detail ('11-4') and the bird color description ('red guy and a green guy') show real game knowledge, which makes Liz's distraction more damning. The boomerang tip is a nice absurdist extra.

jokes.text: Listen, lady... a gender I write extremely well if the story calls for it...
jokes.setup: Sorkin addresses Liz
jokes.punchline: His parenthetical defense of his female character writing — 'if the story calls for it' — is a self-aware dig at the criticism that Sorkin only writes good female characters as supporting figures to male narratives
jokes.explanation: A sharp piece of self-directed industry satire. 'If the story calls for it' is the qualifying clause that undermines the whole defense — it's the kind of thing a writer would say to dodge the charge that he only writes women well when it's convenient to the male protagonist's journey. Sorkin playing himself and allowing this level of roasting is impressive. The joke rewards media-literate viewers.

jokes.text: We make horse buggies, and the first Model T just rolled into town. We're dinosaurs. — We don't need two metaphors. That's bad writing, not that it matters.
jokes.setup: Sorkin makes a mixed metaphor speech about their obsolescence
jokes.punchline: Liz calls out the mixed metaphor; Sorkin dismisses it with 'That's bad writing, not that it matters' — a self-deprecating admission from a famous writer that he just produced bad writing
jokes.explanation: A layered meta-joke: Sorkin (a writer famous for his craft) commits a craft error, gets called on it by another writer, and his response is simultaneously a confession and a nihilistic shrug. 'Not that it matters' is the dark heart of the joke — he's internalized the idea that good writing is becoming irrelevant. Works on multiple levels and is genuinely quotable.

jokes.text: Mr. Lachey, huge fan, huge fan! I've have all your albums!
jokes.setup: The Nick Lachey meeting is announced; Sorkin grandstands about the death of craft
jokes.punchline: Sorkin immediately pivots to sycophantic fandom upon hearing Lachey's name — 'I have all your albums' reveals he's a *NSYNC/Lachey fan, completely undermining his cultural credibility
jokes.explanation: The final puncture of Sorkin's grandiosity. After his entire speech about craft and dinosaurs, his immediate reaction to Nick Lachey is fan excitement. 'I have all your albums' from Aaron Sorkin is a perfect character reversal — it destroys his pretensions in one line and suggests the writing world's nosedive isn't so tragic after all. One of the better beats in the Sorkin sequence.

jokes.text: Oh, you'll be proud of me, Miss Lemon. It is not easy coming up with ideas to save the show, but this morning, I held up this sign in the 'Today Show' window!
jokes.setup: Kenneth promises to save the show
jokes.punchline: His big idea is holding up a sign in the Today Show window — an extremely low-tech, low-impact fan gesture that Kenneth presents with complete pride
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's sunny, hopeless optimism is well-captured here. The visual of him holding up a sign in the Today Show window — and being proud of it — is endearing and funny. The joke's impact depends on Kenneth's specific character; without him, it wouldn't land.

jokes.text: They sent light bulbs to save 'Friday Night Lights,' hot sauce to save 'Roswell,' and douche bags to save 'Entourage.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth explains fan campaigns where items are mailed to networks
jokes.punchline: The escalating list of items ends with 'douche bags to save Entourage' — calling the fans and/or the show itself a douche bag while framing it as a heartfelt campaign
jokes.explanation: A masterfully constructed list joke. The first two items are real and thematically connected (the items relate to the shows' titles), building a pattern. The third breaks the pattern with a cruel punchline that works on multiple levels: the fans chose something that insults themselves, or the show earned that association. Kenneth delivers it with complete earnestness, which is the perfect vehicle. The structural elegance of the list — setup, setup, punchline — is textbook. One of the best jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Bird Internet!
jokes.setup: Kenneth and Liz need to find something fans can send Hank Hooper that represents TGS
jokes.punchline: Kenneth triumphantly proposes 'Bird Internet' — a callback to Liz's useless idea journal — as if it's the answer
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'Bird Internet' works because the idea is no less nonsensical here than when it was in the journal — Kenneth proposing it as a fan campaign item is completely absurd. The two-word economy is at maximum. The rewatch bonus applies because knowing 'Bird Internet' is a running thread makes every instance funnier.

jokes.text: These aren't babies. They're organ farms!
jokes.setup: Jack arrives at Devon Banks's Brooklyn home to find it full of babies
jokes.punchline: Devon's cynical reframe of his own children as 'organ farms' — presumably because he mixed sperm with his husband so the babies can donate to each other — is maximally dark
jokes.explanation: A great character introduction line. 'Organ farms' is both a logical (if monstrous) extension of Banks's calculation and a brilliantly dark piece of absurdist logic. It's delivered immediately upon Jack's arrival, which tells us everything about where Devon Banks is emotionally. High economy, great character integration.

jokes.text: I'm a househusband now. Happy? I married a shiny black dancer named Cashmere. We mixed our sperm together so no one would know whose baby is whose.
jokes.setup: Jack asks Devon to explain the babies
jokes.punchline: Devon's explanation — mixed sperm so paternity is ambiguous — is presented as a practical solution to a problem, delivered with defeated resignation
jokes.explanation: 'Shiny black dancer named Cashmere' is doing a lot of work in this joke — the adjective 'shiny,' the profession, and the name 'Cashmere' are each absurd details. The sperm-mixing logic is presented as a reasonable domestic arrangement, which is the dark-absurdist engine of the joke. Devon's total defeat ('Happy?') is perfect character regression from his former shark persona.

jokes.text: You thought that I would lick your boots, but you need me. So now I'm gonna make you let me lick your boots!
jokes.setup: Devon realizes Jack needs him, giving him leverage
jokes.punchline: His power move is to force Jack to ALLOW him to lick his boots — he's reframing submission as dominance, which is completely incoherent but delivered with full confidence
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character joke. The logical paradox — Devon seizes on his leverage to demand the right to be submissive — is both absurdist and a perfect expression of Banks's character: he will find dominance in any position. The sexual double entendre underneath adds another layer. This is also great setup for the following exchange where Jack continues to accidentally deliver BDSM-coded corporate language.

jokes.text: I'll keep you on a very tight leash. — Fantastic. Continue. — You will be under me, and if there's one slipup, your ass is mine!
jokes.setup: Jack lays out the terms of Banks's employment
jokes.punchline: Every corporate dominance phrase Jack uses — 'tight leash,' 'under me,' 'your ass is mine' — is received by Devon with enthusiastic sexual appreciation, and Jack is too oblivious to stop
jokes.explanation: A great escalating double entendre sequence. The structure relies on Jack's obliviousness — he's delivering standard power-corporate language while Devon receives each line as erotic. 'Fantastic. Continue.' after 'tight leash' is perfect. The escalation of the three phrases ('tight leash' → 'under me' → 'your ass is mine') is well-constructed, with each one being more obviously double-coded. Strong character integration for both.

jokes.text: Devon: 'I'll keep you on a very tight leash.' / Jack: 'Fantastic. Continue.'
jokes.setup: Jack is establishing the power dynamic.
jokes.punchline: Devon enthusiastically agrees to being on a 'tight leash' — revealing this is not a deterrent but an incentive for him.
jokes.explanation: Compact reaction joke — Devon's 'Fantastic. Continue.' is a great delivery reveal. His enthusiasm for the restraint metaphor extends the BDSM subtext thread running through the scene.

jokes.text: Down came the rain and washed the spider out! — No! You are the spider. I am the sun! I dry up all the rain! — Yes! Freeing me, the spider, to climb up the spout again! — You bastard!
jokes.setup: Devon and Jack argue over who has the upper hand in their arrangement
jokes.punchline: They find themselves in an increasingly earnest argument about which character from 'Itsy Bitsy Spider' each of them represents, with Jack losing the nursery rhyme logic battle
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's comedic peak. Two powerful men conducting corporate power negotiations via Itsy Bitsy Spider metaphor is a sublime absurdist concept. The joke escalates perfectly: Banks introduces the metaphor, Jack tries to reassign roles, Banks finds the loophole in Jack's logic — and the nursery rhyme actually supports Banks's interpretation (the sun dries the rain, freeing the spider to climb again). Jack's 'You bastard!' at losing a nursery rhyme argument is the perfect ending. Exceptional structure, originality, and character integration. This is calibrated at the level of the anchor examples.

jokes.text: Now, who wants some num-nums?
jokes.setup: Devon has just outsmarted Jack in the spider metaphor battle
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots from corporate shark mode to baby-talk daddy mode, offering 'num-nums' to his babies — the whiplash from predator to nurturing parent is the joke
jokes.explanation: A perfectly timed beat that works through tonal contrast. Banks has just won a high-stakes power negotiation, and his immediate transition to cooing 'num-nums' at babies is jarring in the best way. Three words doing maximum work. The term 'num-nums' will also callback at the episode's end, earning a rewatch bonus.

jokes.text: [Simon breaks up with Liz as an agent using the same speech he'd use to drop a dog client, including the silent beat]
jokes.setup: Simon says he'll tell Liz what he tells his dog clients when he drops them
jokes.punchline: He then communicates with Liz in the way you'd communicate with a dog — presumably using non-verbal cues, body language, a dismissive gesture — Liz receives this as a complete message
jokes.explanation: A visual beat that's funny on the page but rewards viewing — Simon apparently does something nonverbal (a pat on the head? a dismissive gesture?) that communicates the breakup as if to a dog. The implicit insult is that the dog-client script maps perfectly onto Liz. The pause after 'Simon...' and before the next scene marker is the joke.

jokes.text: The only explanation I can think of is that he keeps stopping to perform good deeds.
jokes.setup: Hank Hooper is annoyed that Devon Banks is almost an hour late to the meeting
jokes.punchline: Jack offers the most charitable possible explanation for his nemesis's tardiness — good deeds — with a straight face, covering for Banks while knowing exactly why he's late
jokes.explanation: Jack covering for Banks by attributing the delay to altruism is a good deadpan irony beat. The absurdity of describing Devon Banks — a documented shark — as someone who might stop to do good deeds is the joke. Jack's commitment to the lie is characterful.

jokes.text: Well, I'm a straight shooter, Jack, except at the urinal. But that's just a little shrapnel side effect from Vietnam.
jokes.setup: Hank declares himself a straight shooter in business
jokes.punchline: He self-corrects to exclude urinal performance, attributing it to Vietnam shrapnel — oversharing a medical detail with complete casualness
jokes.explanation: A very strong Hank joke. The idiomatic 'straight shooter' sets up a literal interpretation that Hank himself introduces, only to immediately provide a urological exception with a Vietnam explanation. The casualness of 'that's just a little shrapnel side effect' — treating this as an obvious and unremarkable medical fact — is the comedic engine. Hank's character is defined by these exact kinds of casual overshares from an earlier era of American masculinity.

jokes.text: I tried to call, but somebody spilled milky all over Daddy's phony. Didn't you, little Mykonos?
jokes.setup: Devon arrives late and apologizes to Hank and Jack
jokes.punchline: His baby-talk excuse — 'milky' on 'Daddy's phony' — addressed to a baby named Mykonos, is a complete tonal mismatch for a corporate power meeting
jokes.explanation: Devon's strategic use of baby-talk in a business meeting is great character comedy. 'Phony' for phone and 'milky' for milk in a boardroom context is the joke; naming the baby 'Mykonos' (a Greek island) is an extra absurd character detail. Banks is using the baby as a prop while maintaining plausible deniability through genuine affection.

jokes.text: of course, I didn't want to miss this fabulous opportunity. I'm always just trying to balance work and family. It's kind of what I'm all about.
jokes.setup: Banks apologizes for being late with his baby at a business meeting
jokes.punchline: Devon performs work-life balance sincerity while clearly and cynically using the baby as a manipulation tool — 'it's kind of what I'm all about' is the most calculated possible thing to say
jokes.explanation: Banks performing 'relatable family man' for Hank Hooper while Jack watches in horror is good dramatic irony comedy. The gap between Devon's authentic shark nature and his performed warmth is the joke. Works especially well because we've seen the 'organ farms' comment.

jokes.text: The VC was everywhere. Yes, they were! Yes, they were!
jokes.setup: Hank stays behind to entertain the baby while Jack and Devon confer
jokes.punchline: Hank tells baby Mykonos a Vietnam War story in the cooing register normally reserved for peek-a-boo — 'The VC was everywhere. Yes, they were! Yes, they were!'
jokes.explanation: The best character joke in the episode and one of the finest Hank Hooper moments the show ever produced. The structure is perfect: baby-talk cadence applied to Vietnam War horror. 'The VC was everywhere' is a statement of genuine trauma; 'Yes, they were! Yes, they were!' is delivered in the exact same delighted tone a grandparent uses for 'peek-a-boo.' The tonal collision is total and instant. Pure Hank — his character contains both his cheerful grandfatherliness and his specific historical context, and this joke merges them completely. Top-tier quotability; this line stands alone outside context.

jokes.text: I brought the sexiest one, too. His cheekbones are like granite.
jokes.setup: Jack accuses Devon of using his baby to manipulate Hank
jokes.punchline: Devon confirms he deliberately selected the most attractive baby for the meeting, evaluating infant cheekbones with talent-scout precision
jokes.explanation: Devon's calm, proud confirmation that he chose the most photogenic baby for the meeting is a great character beat. 'His cheekbones are like granite' as infant modeling critique is both absurd and perfectly Devon. Only a character who described his children as 'organ farms' would evaluate them for business utility by bone structure.

jokes.text: This isn't even baby vomit on my jacket! It's mine! All mine!
jokes.setup: Devon claimed the baby threw up on him as an excuse
jokes.punchline: Revealed: Devon vomited on his own jacket — either from stress or method-acting the paternal role so completely he made himself sick
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Devon's baby vomit was his own is genuinely surprising and darkly committed. 'All mine!' has the exultant energy of a villain monologue, making the confession of self-vomiting even funnier. A twisted detail that reveals how far Devon will go.

jokes.text: 'Whoosh!' went the flamethrower. 'Medic! Medic!' cried the little boy!
jokes.setup: Hank continues entertaining the baby while Jack and Devon argue
jokes.punchline: His Vietnam story — told in children's book cadence — has escalated to flamethrowers and wounded children
jokes.explanation: The callback escalation of Hank's Vietnam baby story. The first beat established the tonal contrast; this one escalates to maximum horror ('Whoosh!' went the flamethrower) while maintaining the same cooing children's-book structure. The onomatopoeia 'Whoosh!' in the cadence of a fairy tale is a brilliant structural choice. 'Medic! Medic! cried the little boy' is maximally dark in this register. This rivals the first beat for impact.

jokes.text: Just like 'Lean on Me,' in that a guy who looks like Morgan Freeman swung a bat at me.
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks how substitute teaching went
jokes.punchline: Pete's reference to 'Lean on Me' (the inspirational Morgan Freeman teacher movie) is immediately clarified as meaning only the bat-swinging — the inspirational reading is rejected for the violent one
jokes.explanation: Mirrors the 'Dead Poets Society / got fired' structure from Pete's earlier joke (id: 13) — Pete uses a flattering film comparison that's immediately deflated by clarifying only the worst aspect applies. The Morgan Freeman bat-swing is a more extreme version of the Dead Poets firing. Good structural symmetry with the earlier Pete joke.

jokes.text: I've already sent about 100 of these, even though licking an envelope is a sin... unless you're married to it. So I had to marry each envelope and then divorce it, which brings me to my ninth point...
jokes.setup: Kenneth is mailing sugar cubes to Hank Hooper as a fan campaign
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's religion prohibits licking envelopes unless married to them, so he's married and divorced 100 envelopes — and this is apparently only the ninth point of a much longer theological digression
jokes.explanation: Peak Kenneth. His religion's prohibition on envelope-licking, the loophole of marriage, the 100 consecutive envelope marriages and divorces, and 'which brings me to my ninth point' — these escalate beautifully. The 'ninth point' is the killer button: we're mid-stream in a Kenneth theological treatise that started long before we arrived. Only Kenneth Parcell has a religion with this specific doctrine. Top character integration score.

jokes.text: Kenneth, do you know what anthrax looks like?
jokes.setup: Liz realizes that sugar cubes mailed to Hank Hooper will be crushed into fine white powder upon arrival
jokes.punchline: Liz's dawning horror culminates in asking Kenneth about anthrax — the fan campaign has become a bioterrorism incident
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured escalation joke. The setup has multiple layers: the sweet idea of sugar cubes, Kenneth's religious complications with envelope-licking, and then Liz's logical realization about crushed sugar = white powder. The anthrax conclusion is the payoff of a chain of comedic logic. Well-constructed and dark.

jokes.text: I'm not with him! God bless America! My thorax!
jokes.setup: Kenneth has apparently been arrested by federal agents due to the white powder mail
jokes.punchline: Kenneth distances himself from Liz as authorities close in, then cries 'My thorax!' — suggesting he's being tackled and references the wrong body part in panic
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's immediate betrayal of Liz ('I'm not with him!' — calling Liz 'him' in a panic) and his very specific screaming about his thorax rather than the expected body part is a great Kenneth character joke. 'My thorax!' implies either an insect-self-identification or Kenneth's weird biology. Quick, punchy, good.

jokes.text: Thank you, Mentaalist. It is a gift and a curse. In the TV show, you bang me in a tulip field under credits.
jokes.setup: The writer who mentioned his Dutch psychic career is apparently being used as a real psychic to track down Kenneth
jokes.punchline: He thanks 'Mentaalist' (a Dutch version of The Mentalist), then reveals his TV counterpart has a specific relationship with the main character involving a tulip field
jokes.explanation: A good callback to the earlier Dutch psychic gag, now deployed practically. 'Mentaalist' as a Dutch show name is a funny detail (extra 'a' for Dutch). The tulip field revelation — a specific romantic encounter under closing credits — adds absurdist world-building to a background character. Good use of a minor running gag.

jokes.text: Mommy, what's that? — It's a toilet or a woman. It's whatever you need it to be.
jokes.setup: A child asks a parent what something is (presumably Liz or a street scene)
jokes.punchline: The parent's answer — 'it's a toilet or a woman, it's whatever you need it to be' — is both absurdly philosophical and deeply offensive in the most casual way
jokes.explanation: A passing street comedy moment. The parent's nihilistic answer to a simple child's question is funny in its philosophical resignation ('it's whatever you need it to be') while also being a casual insult to Liz. The joke is brisk and quick, which is the right approach. Lower character integration because these are one-off characters.

jokes.text: People of the sidewalk, we can't give up on the written word! We need stories. Because I don't have a Plan B! I have a degree in Theater Tech with a minor in Movement! Why did my parents let me do that?
jokes.setup: Liz has a breakdown in the street about the death of writing
jokes.punchline: Her impassioned defense of storytelling collapses immediately into a personal crisis about her Theater Tech degree — the grand quickly becomes the petty
jokes.explanation: A well-structured speech that starts with Sorkin-esque nobility ('People of the sidewalk!') and deflates to a personal parental grievance about a minor in Movement. The joke is in the collapse — Liz cannot maintain dignity even in crisis. 'Why did my parents let me do that?' is the perfect helpless button.

jokes.text: Who's there? Show yourselves! — You're one of us now. — Better to ask who we used to be. — Once, I was called Travel Agent. — I was an American Auto Worker. — And I played dynamite saxophone solos in rock-'n'-roll songs.
jokes.setup: Liz breaks down on the street about having no Plan B
jokes.punchline: She is approached by a Greek chorus of obsolete professionals — a travel agent, auto worker, and rock saxophone soloist — who welcome her into their subterranean community of the economically irrelevant
jokes.explanation: A genuinely inventive absurdist sequence. The three professions are well-curated: travel agent (internet-killed), auto worker (economy-killed), and rock saxophone soloist (culture-killed by a different era). The escalation from real economic displacement to the absurdly specific 'dynamite saxophone solos' is good. The underground community of obsolete professionals is a strong absurdist image.

jokes.text: Come. We live under the subways with the CEO of Friendster.
jokes.setup: The obsolete professionals invite Liz to join their underground community
jokes.punchline: Their community includes the CEO of Friendster — a defunct social network — as its most distinguished resident
jokes.explanation: The Friendster CEO is the episode's most precise cultural joke. Friendster was the original social network, completely eclipsed by MySpace and then Facebook — its CEO is the platonic ideal of someone whose entire industry evaporated. Placing him as the community elder under the subways is a perfect absurdist image. Economy is exceptional: 'the CEO of Friendster' in seven words tells an entire story of technological displacement.

jokes.text: Morning, Jack! Empty coffee pot, same cheap $300 tie as yesterday, nose hair all askew. You've been here all night trying to figure out how to fight back, haven't you?
jokes.setup: Devon arrives the next morning to find Jack already at the office
jokes.punchline: Devon's deduction of Jack's all-nighter from 'nose hair all askew' — among other clues — is both a Sherlock Holmes parody and a deeply specific insult
jokes.explanation: Devon's forensic assessment of Jack's grooming degradation — and specifically 'nose hair all askew' — is good character comedy. Nose hair as the tell for Jack Donaghy's emotional state is a very specific, funny detail. The callback to Hank Hooper's earlier comment about nose hairs being important to a man adds a layer.

jokes.text: Oh, it was amazing. Yes, really superlative tummy time. Oh, I almost forgot. Hank — Uncle Hank — wants to expand overseas, and he's chosen me to be the face of the company in Europe. That's right, I've been promoted.
jokes.setup: Devon innocently describes his playdate with the Hoopers before delivering the killing blow
jokes.punchline: Devon's promotion to European face of KableTown is revealed casually, after establishing enough 'tummy time' warmth that Jack can't immediately object
jokes.explanation: Devon's use of 'tummy time' and 'superlative' in the same breath before delivering a corporate coup is effective character comedy. The tonal whiplash between baby affection and ruthless career maneuvering is Banks's defining comedic mode.

jokes.text: But Europe is my purview! I was supposed to go there next week. I was going to take a picture where it looked like I was holding up the Leaning Tower of Pisa! Now I'll be taking that picture!
jokes.setup: Devon reveals he's been made European director at Jack's expense
jokes.punchline: Jack's specific complaint — losing the Leaning Tower of Pisa tourist photo opportunity — reveals that beneath his corporate gravitas, he is excited about the exact same tourist cliché as everyone else
jokes.explanation: Jack's wounded dignity about Europe is entirely deflated by his specific grief about the Leaning Tower photo — a tourist activity that no one with Jack's self-image should care about. 'Now I'll be taking that picture!' from Devon as a gloating taunt about a tourist photo is a wonderfully petty power move. Great character deconstruction.

jokes.text: I was trapped in a world of wet wipes and rectal thermometers. Then the babies came, and life changed.
jokes.setup: Devon reflects on his domestic period in Brooklyn
jokes.punchline: The phrase 'Then the babies came, and life changed' implies the babies were an escape from the domestic horrors — but the domestic horrors WERE the babies
jokes.explanation: A dark Devon monologue beat — his period of being a househusband is described as imprisonment ('wet wipes and rectal thermometers') and then the babies are presented as his liberation, which is a paradox since the babies were the source of the wet wipes and thermometers. Banks's perspective on his own children is consistently the darkest possible.

jokes.text: Three pairs of grubby little hands smearing food all over your brand-new chihuahua outfits.
jokes.setup: Devon describes the chaos of having triplets
jokes.punchline: The chihuahua outfits callback — established by Liz's D'Fwan reference earlier — implies Devon also owns expensive chihuahua outfits as a gay man, and the babies are ruining them
jokes.explanation: An excellent callback that retroactively deepens the earlier D'Fwan joke. The $4,000 chihuahua outfit joke gains new resonance when Devon (another gay character) is revealed to also own chihuahua outfits — it suggests this is simply a feature of this demographic's consumer behavior. The detail is presented as one of Devon's real parenting hardships, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Three perfect little mouths that smile every time I walk through the door... Three tummies that just want their num-nums and zerberts. Oh, God, I just love my gaybies too much! I can't leave!
jokes.setup: Devon is building to talk himself out of the Europe job through love for his babies
jokes.punchline: Devon Banks — corporate shark, organ farm enthusiast — completely breaks under the weight of genuine parental love, using baby words like 'num-nums' and 'zerberts' while abandoning his scheme
jokes.explanation: A perfect character arc payoff. Devon Banks — who called his children 'organ farms,' chose the 'sexiest' one for a meeting, and just executed a flawless power play — completely capitulates to parental love mid-speech. The 'num-nums' callback from the Brooklyn scene makes this hit harder. The word 'zerberts' (a raspberry on a baby's stomach) in Devon's vocabulary is wonderful. 'I can't leave!' from a character who seemed to have no genuine affection for anyone is a real character moment wrapped in absurdist comedy. Top character integration.

jokes.text: I'm sorry, Jack. But I had stuff planned! I was going to 'Trading Places' you! — Hey, I was bailed out of prison and told to come up here?
jokes.setup: Devon reveals he had an elaborate plan to switch positions with Jack
jokes.punchline: A man appears who was clearly hired to play the 'poor person' role in Banks's Trading Places scheme — he's been bailed out of prison per the movie's plot and is confused
jokes.explanation: Devon's abandoned Trading Places scheme is revealed through its evidence — a confused man who was bailed from prison as part of the plan. 'That was weak, Banks' from Jack after Banks's explanation is the perfect button: Jack is disappointed in the quality of the scheme, not the fact of it. The man's confusion ('Hey, I was bailed out of prison and told to come up here?') is a great absurdist detail.

jokes.text: That was weak, Banks.
jokes.setup: Devon reveals his Trading Places scheme before abandoning it
jokes.punchline: Jack's critique is not that Devon tried to ruin him — that's expected — but that the scheme was below Devon's usual standard
jokes.explanation: Three words that do enormous character work. Jack doesn't object to the scheme itself; he objects to its quality. This establishes their relationship as a kind of mutual professional respect between opponents. The understatement is perfect.

jokes.text: And yet you still managed to be here all night trying to figure out how to bring me down? Damn, Jack. You are strong. You're like Dora's friend. — Benny the Bull. — Benny the Bull.
jokes.setup: Devon realizes Jack spent the night trying to fight back even while being a parent
jokes.punchline: Devon's ultimate compliment for Jack's strength is comparing him to Benny the Bull from Dora the Explorer — a children's cartoon bull character — which Jack immediately identifies, revealing both men watch children's TV
jokes.explanation: Devon's highest compliment for Jack's strength is a Dora the Explorer character reference, and Jack immediately knows who he means. The moment of shared recognition — both power-players knowing children's TV character minutiae — is both humanizing and absurd. 'Benny the Bull' repeated as a moment of mutual acknowledgment is the perfect comedic button. High quotability.

jokes.text: Okay, here's an idea. We keep 'TGS' going as a magazine.
jokes.setup: Liz is trying desperately to save TGS
jokes.punchline: Her best idea is converting a live TV show into a magazine — an industry that is itself dying — which is not a solution but a lateral problem
jokes.explanation: A quick, functional joke about Liz's panic-idea quality. Converting a TV show to a magazine as a solution is bad advice on multiple levels (magazines are also dying). It's a minor beat in a transitional scene.

jokes.text: Here, I'm actually not that hungry.
jokes.setup: Liz apologizes for failing to save the show and gives Kenneth some food
jokes.punchline: Liz voluntarily giving away food is the tell for her genuine emotional distress — the audience knows from the pilot that Liz not being hungry is a crisis indicator
jokes.explanation: A sophisticated character beat that rewards long-time viewers. Liz giving away food is a profound character signal — she is never not hungry. The joke works as understatement: the most devastating admission Liz can make is that she doesn't want pizza. Strong character integration for fans of the show.

jokes.text: This is the same place Mr. Jordan gets pizza from in Africa.
jokes.setup: Kenneth observes the pizza Liz is giving away
jokes.punchline: Tracy gets pizza from the same place — in 'Africa' — which immediately tells us he's not in Africa
jokes.explanation: The plot-resolution joke is also the episode's cleverest structural beat. Kenneth's innocent observation instantly breaks Tracy's cover. The joke's economy is remarkable — one casual pizza comment solves the episode's central mystery. The structure (innocuous setup → world-changing punchline) is near-perfect. Liz's realization beat that follows makes this land even harder.

jokes.text: Africa's great! We got juju monsters... gum-gum trees, and horsicorns, which is a unicorn with a horse's head.
jokes.setup: Tracy is being questioned about Africa while hiding the fact that he's in New York
jokes.punchline: Tracy's 'Africa' contains entirely fictional creatures — juju monsters, gum-gum trees, horsicorns — none of which exist, because he's describing a made-up place
jokes.explanation: Tracy's imaginary Africa is purely his own invention. The three invented things escalate well: 'juju monsters' is vaguely plausible, 'gum-gum trees' is more childlike, and 'horsicorns, which is a unicorn with a horse's head' is the peak of confident nonsense — Tracy defining a horsicorn as a variant of a unicorn that replaces the magical horn with... a horse's head. The definition is both absurd and has a weird internal logic. High quotability.

jokes.text: Kenneth, you beautiful goon! He's not in Africa! He's somewhere in the delivery zone of Federici's Pizza! We can find him and bring him back here!
jokes.setup: Liz realizes Tracy is in New York based on the pizza
jokes.punchline: Liz's detection method — pizza delivery zone — and her affectionate 'beautiful goon' for Kenneth is a good comedic resolution beat
jokes.explanation: The follow-through on the pizza revelation. 'Beautiful goon' is a perfectly Liz way to compliment Kenneth. 'Delivery zone of Federici's Pizza' as a detective tool is funny and specific. Good resolution energy.

jokes.text: And I won't have to be the world's worst hooker! You want to party? It's $500 for kissing, $10,000 for snuggling, end of list.
jokes.setup: Liz celebrates that she won't have to find another job
jokes.punchline: Her backup backup plan was prostitution — but as the world's worst hooker, with a price list that charges vastly more for snuggling than sex and ends abruptly at snuggling
jokes.explanation: An exceptional character joke with a perfect price list. The comedy works on multiple levels: Liz considering prostitution as a fallback, the pricing that values snuggling ($10,000) twenty times more than kissing ($500) and implicitly prices sex below zero since it's not on the list at all, and 'end of list' as a clear indication that intimacy is her absolute limit. The pricing reveals Liz's actual emotional needs. One of the episode's most quotable lines.

jokes.text: No! / I'm hungry again!
jokes.setup: Liz's emotional crisis resolves; she had given away her food earlier when 'not hungry'
jokes.punchline: With the crisis averted, her appetite immediately returns — confirming that her earlier lack of hunger was the emotional crisis signal
jokes.explanation: The perfect button on the episode's food-as-emotional-barometer arc. 'I'm hungry again!' is the resolution of Liz's arc AND a callback to Joke 87 AND the vending machine opener. The callback structure of this episode — opening with Liz's food motivation, using food withdrawal as crisis signal, and hunger return as resolution — is elegant. High character integration.

jokes.text: Have you made friends in Africa? — Oh, sure. Ladysmith Black Mambazo, Paul Simon, 'Invictus.'
jokes.setup: Tracy's cover is about to be blown; he's asked about Africa friends
jokes.punchline: Tracy lists his 'Africa friends' — a famous South African choir, a famous American musician who worked with them, and a movie about South Africa — two of which aren't people and none of which are actually friends
jokes.explanation: Tracy's Africa friends list — including a film as a friend — is good Tracy-logic. The escalation from a real entity (Ladysmith) to a person associated with them (Paul Simon) to a movie (Invictus) follows a degrading logic of Tracy's Africa knowledge.

jokes.text: So, what's the weather like? — Crazy. It's the snowiest winter we had in years in New York... in Africa.
jokes.setup: Tracy is asked about weather in 'Africa'
jokes.punchline: He accidentally says 'New York' before correcting to 'Africa' — the tell that undoes everything
jokes.explanation: A clean Freudian slip joke. Tracy's correction — 'in New York... in Africa' — is almost but not quite smooth enough, and the delay before 'in Africa' lands the comedy. The 'snowiest winter' also inadvertently confirms a New York winter, not an equatorial one. Good escalation of his cover falling apart.

jokes.text: Uh-oh, it's nighttime. Got to go to bed or I'll anger the gods. They must be crazy! Africa!
jokes.setup: Tracy's cover is unraveling and he needs to end the conversation
jokes.punchline: His excuse for hanging up — angering the gods — transitions into a reference to the movie 'The Gods Must Be Crazy' (a South African film), and 'Africa!' as a sign-off
jokes.explanation: Tracy's cultural reference pivot from 'anger the gods' to 'The Gods Must Be Crazy' is a good Tracy-brain association joke. 'Africa!' as a conversational sign-off is a funny piece of Tracy-speak. His desperation to end the conversation while maintaining the ruse is good comedic energy.

jokes.text: I probably should have realized he was in New York sooner.
jokes.setup: Tracy's cover is completely blown
jokes.punchline: Liz's self-assessment is understated acknowledgment that the pizza-delivery zone clue was the least she should have caught
jokes.explanation: A good button for the Tracy reveal sequence. Liz's understatement implies there were earlier, more obvious tells she also missed. Functional and characterful but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Bird internet. [Final scene: the idea journal callback]
jokes.setup: The episode is closing; the 'Bird Internet' concept has been bouncing around all episode
jokes.punchline: The episode ends on 'Bird Internet' — it never becomes a real idea, it's never explained, it simply is — the final statement of the episode's most absurdist recurring non-joke
jokes.explanation: The episode's closing joke. 'Bird Internet' works as a callback payoff precisely because it doesn't pay off — the concept remains as meaningless at the end as it was in Liz's journal. The joke is that it keeps returning without ever becoming real. Using it as the literal final word of the episode is a bold, confident structural choice. The absurdist void of 'Bird Internet' as an episode thesis is very 30 Rock. Near-maximum economy (two words, zero meaning, everything implied).

tmdb_overview: "TGS" is forced into hiatus, spurring the show's staffers to seek backup jobs. Meanwhile, Jack tries to rescue a cable network by forging an unlikely alliance with his archenemy, Devin Banks.
insight: Absurdist comedy carries a 87-point episode with nearly 3 jokes per minute across 75 gags.
